qs.q: A patient with diabetes mellitus has a fasting plasma glucose of 180 mg/dL. The laboratory uses a hexokinase method to measure glucose. What is the primary advantage of this method over the glucose oxidase method?
o: Faster reaction time allowing for rapid results
Lower cost associated with reagents and equipment
Higher specificity for glucose over other hexoses
Complete lack of interference from ascorbic acid
Ability to measure total carbohydrate content
qs.e: The hexokinase method is highly specific for glucose, minimizing interference from other sugars like galactose or fructose.

qs.q: A patient is evaluated for glycemic status and found to have a fasting plasma glucose level of 115 mg/dL (6.4 mmol/L). How should this finding be categorized?
o: Impaired fasting glucose diagnostic of prediabetes
Normal upper limit of fasting blood glucose level
Impaired glucose tolerance based on oral load
Provisional diagnosis of established type diabetes
qs.e: Prediabetes is defined by impaired fasting glucose when fasting glucose is between 100 and 125 mg/dL. A fasting concentration of 99 mg/dL or lower represents the upper limit of normal.

qs.q: A 55-year-old man presents with episodic diaphoresis, tremulousness, and confusion that consistently resolve after drinking orange juice. Laboratory evaluation reveals a fasting plasma glucose level of 42 mg/dL. Which constellation of findings confirms this diagnosis?
o: Postprandial glucose of 140 mg/dL, elevated C-peptide, and lack of symptom relief with feeding
Fasting glucose above 126 mg/dL, metabolic acidosis, and positive urinary acetoacetate
Symptoms during fasting, concurrent glucose below 50 mg/dL, and resolution after carbohydrate intake
Serum osmolarity over 320 mOsm/L, normal pH, and severe dehydration without ketosis
qs.e: Whipple's triad requires hypoglycemic symptoms, low plasma glucose during symptoms, and relief when glucose is restored. The other sets describe diabetic ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar states, or non-hypoglycemic conditions.

qs.q: A 38-year-old healthcare worker presents with recurrent symptomatic hypoglycemia, a low fasting plasma glucose level, and markedly elevated serum insulin. What is the primary diagnostic utility of measuring serum C-peptide in this patient?
o: Differentiating autoimmune insulin antibodies from insulin receptor gene mutations
Assessing acute hepatic glycogen breakdown secondary to excessive glucagon secretion
Evaluating total functional beta-cell reserve prior to initiating sulfonylurea therapy
Distinguishing endogenous hyperinsulinism from exogenous insulin administration
qs.e: C-peptide is co-secreted with endogenous insulin in equimolar amounts, so a low C-peptide with high insulin indicates exogenous administration, whereas elevated C-peptide indicates endogenous hyperinsulinism. Evaluating beta-cell reserve is used in managing established diabetes rather than diagnosing acute hypoglycemia.

qs.q: Diagnostic criterion for diabetes mellitus using fasting plasma glucose is ---
o: B. ≥ 7.8 mmol/L
A. ≥ 6.1 mmol/L
D. ≥ 6.5 mmol/L
C. ≥ 7.0 mmol/L
qs.e: A fasting plasma glucose of 7.0 mmol/L or higher meets the diagnostic threshold for diabetes.

qs.q: The diagnostic criterion for diabetes mellitus using fasting plasma glucose is
o: ≥6.1 mmol/L (110 mg/dL)
≥11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) on any sample
≥8.0 mmol/L (144 mg/dL)
≥7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL)
qs.e: WHO/ADA: FPG ≥7.0 mmol/L on two occasions = diabetes (option D is also valid on a symptomatic random sample).

ai.title: Fasting Plasma Glucose for Diabetes Diagnosis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) measures blood glucose after an overnight fast, primarily used to screen for and diagnose diabetes mellitus and pre-diabetes. It reflects baseline glucose control and is a key diagnostic criterion alongside other tests. Understanding FPG helps clinicians identify metabolic dysfunction early.

sections.p: Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) is a measurement of glucose levels in the blood after an overnight fast, typically 8-12 hours. It is a cornerstone in the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and pre-diabetes. The diagnosis of diabetes requires specific criteria, often involving FPG.
b: A fasting period of at least 8 hours (but not more than 12 hours) is essential for an accurate FPG result.
Diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus (any one of the following):
Fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L (or ≥126 mg/dL).
Random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (or ≥200 mg/dL) with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia.
HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or more.
Pre-diabetes (Impaired Fasting Glucose, IFG) is diagnosed with an FPG of 5.6-6.9 mmol/L (or 100-125 mg/dL).

sections.p: FPG helps classify glucose dysregulation into normal, pre-diabetes, or diabetes. It does not directly stage the severity of diabetes complications, but a higher FPG value generally indicates poorer glycemic control and a greater risk of complications.
b: Normal: FPG <5.6 mmol/L (<100 mg/dL).
Pre-diabetes (Impaired Fasting Glucose): FPG 5.6-6.9 mmol/L (100-125 mg/dL). This indicates increased risk for developing type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
Diabetes Mellitus: FPG ≥7.0 mmol/L (≥126 mg/dL). This confirms the diagnosis of diabetes.

sections.p: Elevated FPG primarily results from impaired insulin production, insulin resistance, or both. Understanding the underlying cause guides management.
b: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Most common cause, characterized by insulin resistance and progressive beta-cell dysfunction.
Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, leading to absolute insulin deficiency.
Gestational Diabetes: Glucose intolerance first recognized during pregnancy, often due to hormonal changes causing insulin resistance.
Secondary Diabetes: Caused by other conditions or medications, such as:
Pancreatic diseases (e.g., pancreatitis, hemochromatosis, cystic fibrosis).
Endocrine disorders (e.g., Cushing's syndrome, acromegaly, hyperthyroidism).
Medications (e.g., corticosteroids, thiazide diuretics, some antipsychotics).
Severe stress (e.g., trauma, sepsis, myocardial infarction) can cause transient hyperglycemia.

sections.p: Patients with elevated FPG, especially in the diabetic range, may present with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia. However, many individuals, particularly with pre-diabetes or early type 2 diabetes, are asymptomatic.
b: Polyuria (frequent urination) due to osmotic diuresis.
Polydipsia (increased thirst) compensating for fluid loss.
Polyphagia (increased hunger) despite adequate food intake.
Unexplained weight loss (especially in type 1 diabetes).
Fatigue and lethargy.
Blurred vision.
Recurrent infections (e.g., skin infections, candidiasis).
Slow-healing sores.

sections.p: FPG is a primary diagnostic test. Other investigations help confirm the diagnosis, differentiate types of diabetes, and assess for complications.

t.b: Answers: Is there hyperglycemia after an overnight fast? Result: ≥7.0 mmol/L (≥126 mg/dL) indicates diabetes; 5.6-6.9 mmol/L (100-125 mg/dL) indicates pre-diabetes.

Answers: Is there significant hyperglycemia at any time, especially with symptoms? Result: ≥11.1 mmol/L (≥200 mg/dL) with classic symptoms suggests diabetes. If FPG is unavailable, RPG can be a quick initial screen.

Answers: What is the average blood glucose over the past 2-3 months? Result: ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%) indicates diabetes. Useful for diagnosis and long-term monitoring. May not be available in all low-resource settings; if so, rely more on FPG and OGTT.

t.a: Urine Dipstick for Glucose and Ketones
t.b: Answers: Is there glucose spilling into the urine (glycosuria) or ketone production (ketonuria)? Result: Glycosuria suggests hyperglycemia. Ketonuria suggests severe insulin deficiency (e.g., DKA risk in type 1 diabetes). A quick, low-cost screening tool.

Answers: Is the pancreas producing insulin? Result: Low C-peptide suggests type 1 diabetes or advanced type 2 diabetes with significant beta-cell failure. Often not available in low-resource settings.

sections.p: Uncontrolled high FPG is a marker for diabetes and its acute and chronic complications. Recognizing these red flags is crucial for timely intervention.
b: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): Severe hyperglycemia, metabolic acidosis, and ketonemia, often in type 1 diabetes. Presents with Kussmaul breathing, abdominal pain, altered mental status.
Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS): Severe hyperglycemia without significant ketosis, leading to profound dehydration, often in type 2 diabetes. Presents with altered mental status, seizures.
Hypoglycemia: Can occur with diabetes treatment, leading to confusion, tremors, sweating, loss of consciousness.
Microvascular complications: Retinopathy (vision loss), nephropathy (kidney failure), neuropathy (nerve damage, leading to foot ulcers).
Macrovascular complications: Cardiovascular disease (MI, stroke), peripheral artery disease.
Increased susceptibility to infections: Especially skin, urinary tract, and tuberculosis.

sections.p: Management of elevated FPG focuses on achieving glycemic control to prevent acute and chronic complications. This involves lifestyle modifications and, often, pharmacotherapy.
b: Lifestyle modifications: Cornerstone of management for pre-diabetes and diabetes.
Dietary changes: Reduce refined carbohydrates, sugary drinks; increase fiber, lean protein.
Regular physical activity: Improves insulin sensitivity.
Weight loss: Especially for overweight/obese individuals.
Pharmacotherapy (for diabetes):
Metformin: First-line for type 2 diabetes, reduces hepatic glucose production and improves insulin sensitivity.
Sulfonylureas (e.g., Glibenclamide): Stimulate insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells. Risk of hypoglycemia.
Insulin: Essential for type 1 diabetes; often needed for type 2 diabetes when oral agents are insufficient.

Other agents (e.g., SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists): May be used if available and appropriate, offering additional benefits like cardiovascular protection, but often less accessible in low-resource settings.
Treat underlying causes: Address secondary causes of hyperglycemia (e.g., stop offending medications, manage endocrine disorders).

sections.p: Regular monitoring of FPG and other glycemic parameters is vital. Prevention strategies focus on lifestyle changes to avert or delay the onset of type 2 diabetes.
b: Regular FPG monitoring: To assess glycemic control and adjust treatment.
HbA1c monitoring: Every 3-6 months to assess long-term control (if available).
Screening for complications: Regular eye exams, foot exams, kidney function tests.
Patient education: Emphasize self-management, diet, exercise, medication adherence, and recognizing hypoglycemia/hyperglycemia symptoms.
Prevention of type 2 diabetes: Intensive lifestyle interventions are highly effective in individuals with pre-diabetes.
Annual FPG screening for individuals at high risk (e.g., family history, obesity, previous gestational diabetes).

sections.p: It's important to distinguish FPG from other glucose measurements and conditions that might present similarly.
b: Random Plasma Glucose (RPG): FPG requires a fast, RPG does not. RPG can diagnose diabetes if ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms, but FPG is preferred for screening.
Postprandial Glucose: Glucose measured after a meal. FPG reflects baseline, while postprandial reflects glucose metabolism after food intake.
Hypoglycemia: While FPG measures high glucose, clinicians must also be aware of low glucose, which can cause similar neurological symptoms.
Stress Hyperglycemia: Transient elevation of glucose due to acute illness or injury, which may resolve once the stressor is managed. Requires careful interpretation to avoid misdiagnosing diabetes.

sections.p: Several factors can influence FPG results, leading to inaccurate diagnoses or management decisions.
b: Insufficient fasting: Eating or drinking anything other than water before the test will falsely elevate FPG.
Prolonged fasting: Fasting for more than 12 hours can sometimes lead to lower FPG due to glucose utilization.
Acute illness/stress: Can transiently elevate FPG (stress hyperglycemia), requiring re-testing when the patient is well.
Medications: Steroids, diuretics, and some antipsychotics can increase FPG.
Laboratory errors: Improper sample handling, delay in processing, or incorrect calibration can affect results.
Pregnancy: FPG criteria for gestational diabetes are often lower than for non-pregnant individuals.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of excessive thirst and urination
Blurred vision or sudden vision changes
Confusion, lethargy, or altered mental status
Severe abdominal pain with vomiting in a diabetic patient

faq.q: What is the ideal fasting period for FPG?
faq.a: An ideal fasting period is 8 to 12 hours. Drinking only water is permitted during this time.
Yes, an FPG of ≥7.0 mmol/L (≥126 mg/dL) on two separate occasions, or once if accompanied by classic symptoms, is sufficient for diagnosis.

faq.q: What if FPG is elevated but HbA1c is normal?
faq.a: This could indicate pre-diabetes (Impaired Fasting Glucose) or early diabetes. Further testing like an OGTT may be warranted, or repeat FPG and HbA1c in a few months.

exam: A 45-year-old woman presents with polyuria and polydipsia for 3 months. Her FPG is 6.5 mmol/L. What is your next step in diagnosis and why? — Next step: Perform an Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) or check HbA1c. Her FPG is in the pre-diabetes range (Impaired Fasting Glucose), but her symptoms suggest diabetes. An OGTT would assess her post-glucose load metabolism, or HbA1c would give an average glucose over 2-3 months, to confirm or rule out diabetes.

You are on a ward round in a rural hospital. A patient with severe pneumonia has a random plasma glucose of 15 mmol/L. How do you interpret this, and what is your immediate management? — Interpretation: This is likely stress hyperglycemia due to the severe infection. Immediate management: Treat the pneumonia aggressively. Monitor blood glucose closely; insulin may be needed to control hyperglycemia if persistent, but avoid immediately diagnosing diabetes. Re-evaluate glucose

A patient with newly diagnosed diabetes has an FPG of 8.2 mmol/L. What is your initial management plan, assuming no acute complications? — Initial management: Lifestyle modifications (dietary changes, exercise, weight loss). Start Metformin, if not contraindicated, as it is first-line for type 2 diabetes. Educate the patient on self-monitoring and symptoms of hypoglycemia/hyperglycemia. Plan for follow-up to assess glycemic control.

What are the limitations of using FPG as the sole diagnostic test for diabetes, especially in low-resource settings? — Limitations: FPG only reflects fasting glucose, missing impaired glucose tolerance. It requires patient compliance with fasting. Acute illness can falsely elevate it. It doesn't provide information on long-term control like HbA1c. In low-resource settings, repeat testing might be difficult, and other tests like OGTT or HbA1c might be unavailable.

A patient with known type 2 diabetes on Glibenclamide presents with confusion and sweating. Her FPG is 2.8 mmol/L. What is the most likely cause and immediate action? — Most likely cause: Hypoglycemia induced by Glibenclamide, which stimulates insulin secretion. Immediate action: Administer oral glucose (e.g., sugary drink, glucose tablets) if conscious and able to swallow. If unconscious, administer IV dextrose or IM glucagon. Differentiate between Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG) and Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT). Why is this distinction clinically important? — IFG is diagnosed by FPG 5.6-6.9 mmol/L. IGT is diagnosed by a 2-hour plasma glucose of 7.8-11.0 mmol/L during an OGTT, with a normal FPG. Clinically important: Both are pre-diabetes states, indicating increased risk for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
